key_bets: Sheared-flow stabilization remains effective as pinch lifetime is extended 5-10x from demonstrated 20-40 µs to the 200 µs required for Q > 10
Fusion gain Q > 10 is achievable at 1.2-1.5 MA and 30-35 keV, as calculated but never experimentally demonstrated at any scale
Repetition rate can be scaled from Century's 0.2 Hz to the commercial target of 10 Hz while maintaining electrode, liquid metal, and gas injection reliability
Flowing LiPb can serve simultaneously as first wall, outer electrode, tritium breeder, and neutron shield with TBR ~1.1 in a 3 m blanket using natural (unenriched) lithium
Pulsed power driver wall-to-plasma efficiency of ~70% holds at commercial scale (2-3 MJ/pulse, 10 Hz continuous)
Electrode erosion under 14 MeV neutron bombardment and 10 Hz, 1 MA arcing yields a commercially viable replacement interval, extrapolating from industrial arc-furnace cathode analogues
Modular 50 MWe architecture (10+ modules per plant) delivers O&M and learning benefits without prohibitive common-mode failure or coordination penalties
eliminated_costs: REBCO HTS tape and all superconducting magnet costs — the dominant capital item in compact/spherical tokamak designs is entirely absent
Cryogenic plant: no liquid helium, cold mass, or quench protection systems
Auxiliary heating systems — no NBI beam dumps, gyrotrons, or RF launchers required
Divertor subsystem in the conventional sense — LiPb flowing wall subsumes plasma-facing and heat-exhaust functions
Beryllium first-wall material — LiPb serves directly as the first wall
novel_costs: Pulsed power driver (capacitor banks, pulse-forming networks, high-voltage switches) at ~50-60% of overnight capital, replacing magnets as the dominant capital item
High-duty-cycle electrode system with neutron-hardened materials and frequent replacement under 10 Hz, 1 MA, D-T conditions
Flowing LiPb quadruple-duty subsystem combining first wall, electrode, tritium breeder, and shield — with associated pumping, film-replenishment, and activation management
Capacitor and high-voltage switch supply chain buildout: 10,000-216,000 capacitors per plant with 4-6 year lead times and a 4-6 order-of-magnitude component-lifetime gap
Tritium extraction and inventory management from circulating LiPb at commercial throughput, with activation product handling for Pb/Bi isotopes

risks.description: Q > 10 has never been demonstrated; entire commercial power balance is anchored on calculation, and at Q=5 recirculating fraction exceeds 70% making net output marginal
Pinch lifetime must extend 5-10x from demonstrated 20-40 µs to 200 µs while sheared-flow stabilization continues to work at higher fusion performance
Repetition rate scaling from Century's 0.2 Hz to commercial 10 Hz (50x gap) simultaneously stresses electrodes, liquid metal dynamics, gas injection, and pulsed-power heat rejection
Pulsed power component lifetime shortfall: capacitors demonstrate 10^4-10^5 shots vs. 10^8-10^9 required, a 4-6 order-of-magnitude gap requiring decades-long materials R&D
No commercial high-voltage switch meets the 50-200 kV, 100-200 kA Z-pinch specification — a capability gap requiring a new switch technology class
Capacitor supply chain buildout for a 150-plant fleet would take 125-250 years at current Western manufacturing capacity, with 4-6 year delivery lead times per order
Capital cost entirely uncharacterized in public literature; no independent techno-economic analysis exists for the SFS Z-pinch approach
Electrode erosion rate under 14 MeV neutron bombardment at commercial duty cycle is unmeasured; replacement interval and cost could swing LCOE by ~30% in sensitivity sweeps
LiPb flowing first-wall has no validated fusion analogue; TBR of 1.1 is marginal and a 10% flow-condition reduction could push the plant tritium-negative
Tritium supply chain constraint shared with all D-T concepts: CANDU global production ~1-2 kg/year limits fleet startup inventory
Plant availability and capacity factor have no operational precedent for pulsed Z-pinch; 0.60-0.85 range swings LCOE by ~25%
Thermal conversion efficiency constrained by LiPb solidification floor (~235°C); exact steam Rankine cycle design unpublished
Regulatory pathway novel — LiPb flowing electrode and absence of containment magnets lack licensed precedents, potentially requiring new frameworks
Multi-module architecture introduces coordination complexity and common-mode failure risk across 10+ modules per plant
Tungsten supply for electrodes is ~80% China-dominated, a moderate geopolitical concentration risk shared with tokamak divertor programs
LiPb activation produces Pb-204/205 and bismuth isotopes requiring long-term radioactive waste management of circuit components
